title: TA9-22822
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The minor claimants, XXXXXXX XXXXXX and XXXXXX XXXXXX, are citizens of Hungary, and claim refugee protection pursuant to ss. 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. The mother of the minor claimants, XXXXX XXXXXX, was appointed the Designated Representative for the purpose of their claims.

The designated representative fears persecution at the hands of XXXX XXXX whom, she alleges, would also harm the minor claimants if they were to return to Hungary. The minor claimant XXXXX arrived in Canada on XXXXX, 2009. The DR and the minor claimant XXXX arrived in Canada on XXXXX, 2009. The DR filed a claim for refugee protection on behalf of the minor claimants on November 4, 2009.

The Panel finds that the claimants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection. In arriving at my decision, I have taken into account the Chairperson's Gender Guidelines.1 ANALYSIS
The claimants' identities are established through the oral testimony of the designated representative and the supporting documentation2 filed. Issues of Credibility

When the Designated Representative arrived in Canada on XXXXX, 2009, she provided false information to the Immigration Officer. Officer: Have you been to Canada before? D.R.: No. Officer: Are you sure? D.R.: Well, yes, I have been here before. Officer: Why did you change your name? D.R.: I changed my name prior to coming to Canada. Officer: Was the purpose trying to disclose your prior presence to Canada? D.R.: Yes. Officer: Did you abandon or withdraw your case in 2001? What happened? D.R.: My ex-husband beat me up, he got arrested. I went to immigration and said I wanted to go home. Officer: So you withdrew your application. D.R.: Yes Officer: Did you ever contact the Canadian Embassy or anyone to obtain consent to come to Canada? D.R.: No.3

In her narrative on behalf of the minor claimants4, the designated representative stated that she originally came to Canada in XXXXX of 1999. The agent of persecution, whom the DR had met in Hungary, also arrived in Canada in XXXXX of 1999. The DR stated that she and the agent of persecution had a relationship while living together in Canada.

The DR states in her narrative that her relationship with the agent of persecution became abusive and that he was arrested and convicted in Hamilton, Ontario to 18 months in jail for assault5. The agent of persecution was deported back to Hungary in 2002. The DR herself returned to Hungary in 2001.

The DR states that in XXXXX 2002 the agent of persecution found the DR, forced her to live in an apartment and in XXXXX of 2003, forced her into prostitution on the streets. She continued this work until XXXXX 2004 when she met XXXXX XXXXX with whom she began to live together and in XXXXX of 2005, the claimant XXXXX was born to them. XXXXX came to Canada in XXXX of 2008 but returned to Hungary four months later in XXXXX of the same year and the DR became pregnant with XXXXX. The DR had no contact with the agent of persecution between XXXXX 2004 and XXXXX 2009 when the DR found a note in her mailbox that said: "I told you that I would find you."

The DR then stated that in XXXX of 2009 as she was walking on the street with XXXXX, a car sped by and hit XXXXX. She took him to the hospital where they provided medical assistance.6 In her oral testimony, the DR stated that the doctors wanted the child to remain in the hospital for observation but that he did not want to stay because he was afraid. The Panel pointed out that in paragraph #22 of her written narrative she had written that she had received a phone call from the agent of persecution instructing her to tell the authorities that her son had received his injuries because he had run in front of a car. She wrote that she was terrified and checked the boy out from the hospital against their advice. The Panel asked the DR to explain the discrepancy. She replied that when the doctor said he wanted him to stay in the hospital for observation that's when he became afraid.

I reject this explanation. It would be reasonable to expect someone to have remembered that she had received a threatening telephone call from the agent of persecution when she was at the hospital with her son and to have mentioned it in her oral testimony. The discrepancy between the written testimony and the oral testimony is a major one. In her written statement, the DR stated that she was afraid of keeping the child in the hospital. In her oral testimony, the DR twice stated that the child was the one who was afraid to remain the hospital. The DR provided no reasonable explanation for the discrepancy. I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the DR did not receive a threatening telephone call from the agent of persecution while her son was at the hospital and I also find that the agent of persecution was not the cause of XXXXX's injuries in XXXXX of 2009.

The DR was asked if she had reported this incident to the police and she said no, because she had received the threatening telephone call. I have already made a credibility finding with respect to the threatening telephone call.

The DR then stated that in XXXXX of 2009 she and XXXXX were abducted outside of their home. She stated that they were taken to a room where she was sexually assaulted several times. She was asked how long she had stayed in the apartment and she said two and a half days.

The Panel pointed out that when describing this incident in her written narrative7 she had written that the agent of persecution had let her go the day after the abduction. She was asked to explain the discrepancy. She said that she was there for two days. I reject this explanation. The DR has given three different answers as to how long she had been abducted in XXXX of 2009. In her written narrative she wrote that she was let go the day after the abduction. In her oral testimony, at first she said she was held for two and half days. When confronted with the discrepancy she stated she had been held for two days. The DR provided no reasonable explanation for the discrepancies in her testimony. It is reasonable to expect someone who has been abducted and sexually assaulted to provide a consistent answer when describing the length of her abduction.

Furthermore, the DR stated in her oral testimony that after she was released by the agent of persecution, she and her son took a bus back home. The Panel pointed out to the DR that in her written narrative8 she wrote that the agent of persecution had sent her back home with three men and was asked to explain the discrepancy. The DR stated that three men took her to the bus.

I reject this explanation. The DR has provided different answers as to how she returned home after allegedly being held captive. In her written narrative she wrote that three men brought her home. In her oral testimony she said that she took the bus home. When confronted with the discrepancy she stated that the men took her to the bus. The DR has failed to provide a reasonable explanation for her discrepancy.

Given that the DR was not able to provide a reasonable explanation for the discrepancies in her testimony when describing the alleged abduction and alleged sexual assault, I find on a balance of probabilities, that the DR and XXXXX were not abducted by the agent of persecution nor was she sexually assaulted by the agent of persecution.

The DR was asked if she had reported this incident to the police and she said that she had gone to the police. She was asked if she had a copy of the police report and she stated that she had the report back in Hungary but had no one to get it for her.

I reject this explanation. The DR had a copy of the hospital report with respect to the XXXX 2009 incident. She had made a refugee claim in 2000 and was aware of the importance of providing documentation to the Board. Furthermore, after the hearing, counsel for the minor claimants was given time to provide the Board written submissions. Even with this extra time available to counsel and the DR, no police report was provided to the Board.
The Panel finds that the DR has failed to substantiate her testimony with pertinent documents and did not corroborate the refugee claims of the minors with credible and trustworthy evidence.9

The DR testified that she continued to receive threatening telephone calls from the agent of persecution and that she called the police to report these calls and was told that she had to attend at the police station in person, which she did not do.

The determinative issue in this claim is state protection. In arriving at its decision, the Panel considered the issue of whether the minor claimants' fears are objectively reasonable. In order to do so, the Panel considered whether or not there is adequate state protection in Hungary, whether or not the DR took all reasonable steps on behalf of the minor claimants to avail herself of that protection, and whether she has provided clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect.

There was no persuasive evidence that the minor claimants were mistreated because of their Roma ethnicity. The DR stated that the agent of persecution would use the claimants to take revenge against her and, because of their Roma ethnicity, there is no state protection for the minor claimants if they were to return to Hungary. The DR stated that she reported the incident of XXXX 2009 to the police. I have already made a finding of credibility with respect to that incident. I have also made a finding of credibility with respect to the DR's testimony that she reported the incident of XXXX 2009 to the police. With respect to the threatening telephone calls which the DR alleges to have received prior to arriving in Canada, she testified that she did not attend at a police station in person to make the complaint as requested by the authorities.

I find on a balance of probabilities, that the claimants have not established that state protection is unavailable for them in Hungary. There is a presumption that a state is capable of protecting its citizens. The claimant may rebut this presumption by providing "clear and convincing" proof of lack of state protection in their country of origin. The claimant must approach his or her state for protection, providing state protection might be reasonably forthcoming.10 Evidence that protection being offered is not necessarily perfect11 is not clear and convincing proof of the state's inability to protect its citizens, as no government can guarantee the protection of all its citizens at all times. However, where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authority in place and makes serious efforts to protects its citizens, the mere fact it is not always successful at doing so will not be enough to justify a claim that the victims are unable to avail themselves of protection.12 The onus is on the claimant to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that state protection is inadequate.13

When the state in question is a democratic state, the claimant must do more than simply show that he or she went to see some member of the police force and that his or her efforts were unsuccessful. The burden for the claimant to prove an absence of state protection is directly proportional to the level of democracy of that state. In an established democracy, such as Hungary, the claimant must do more than merely show that he or she went to see members of the police force and that those efforts were unsuccessful. The more democratic the state's institutions, the greater the onus on the claimant to show he or she has exhausted all courses of action available.14 Moreover, local failures by the authorities to provide protection do not mean that the state as a whole fails to protect its citizens, unless the failures form part of a broader pattern of state inability or refusal to provide protection.15 Therefore, a claimant must do more than approach one police officer unsuccessfully before deciding that state protection would not be forthcoming. There is an onus on the claimant to exhaust all courses of action reasonably available to him.16

The documentary evidence before the Board17 indicates that Hungary is a democracy and that there are free and fair elections.18 There is a relatively independent and impartial judiciary.19 Hungary is a member of the European Union. Hungary is in control of its territory and has functioning security forces, both military and police, in place. There is no evidence of a total breakdown of state authority in the country. Therefore, the burden of attempting to show that one should not be required to exhaust all avenues of domestic recourse is a heavy one.20

In his written21 submissions, counsel argued that state protection in Hungary for members of the Roma ethnic group is not adequate. Documents submitted by both the claimant22 and the Board23 do indicate that Hungary has had a history of discrimination against Roma people. However, the documentary evidence currently before the Board indicates that Hungary is attempting to correct its historical discrimination against the Roma people. In particular, I note the report of the European Commission against Racism and Intolerance adopted on June 20, 2008.24 The Commission is an independent human rights monitoring body and is composed of independent and impartial members.25

The report lists a number of initiatives that the Hungarian government has made in its attempt to eradicate discrimination and racism in the country. Although the existence of right wing political organizations that adopt a xenophobic agenda is part of the Democratic process, the Hungarian government has taken several steps to limit and ban the activities of these groups.26

Several attempts have been made by the Hungarian Government to amend its Criminal Code to criminalize hate speech. However, the Hungarian Supreme Court has ruled as unconstitutional these attempts by the Government to restrict and criminalize hate speech.27 The Criminal Code does have other provisions which may be used in hate motivated crimes28.

The report also notes that the government is taking active steps to change the attitude and treatment of members of the police force toward minorities, especially Roma. Training in human rights, basic freedoms, tolerance and how to deal with on the spot cases involving minority groups is being provided both at the Police Academy and medium level in-service police training29.

The government has also introduced significant legislation to combat racial discrimination. The Equal Treatment and Promotion of Equal Opportunities Act was enacted in December of 2003. Among other requirements, the Act prohibits both direct and indirect discrimination on 19 express grounds, such as employment, health care, social security, etc., and it also provides for the setting up of The Equal Treatment Authority which is a body in charge of ensuring compliance with the principle of the legislation.30 The Parliamentary Commissioner for the Rights of National and Ethnic Minorities provides recourse to members of national and ethnic minorities with respect to unconstitutional practices.31 In 1993 the Hungarian Government enacted the Rights of National and Ethnic Minorities which is a comprehensive and progressive tool for the protection of the rights of minorities. Amendments to the Act in 2005 provided for minority self government at the local level32.

The report also outlines the efforts which the Hungarian Government is making to eradicate discrimination in a number of social fields: education, employment, housing, health, and access to public places.33 In June of 2007, the Hungarian Parliament adopted a resolution on the Decade of Roma Inclusion Programme Strategic Plan for 2007-2015. This Resolution sets out a series of tasks to be accomplished in the fields noted above.34

It is accepted that Hungary has had difficulties in the past with addressing racism and discrimination against Roma. However, I find that the documentary evidence cited previously is drawn from a variety of reliable and independent sources, none of which have any vested interest in the outcome of this claim. To that extent it is relatively free of bias. While there are some inconsistencies among sources, the preponderance of the objective evidence regarding current country conditions suggests that, although not perfect, there is adequate state protection in Hungary, that Hungary is making serious and genuine efforts to address the problem of racism.
The claimants have not established that were they to return to Hungary today, protection would not be reasonably forthcoming or that it is objectively unreasonable for them to seek that protection.

I find that, on a balance of probabilities, the claimants have failed to rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence and, as the issue of state protection is equally applicable to claims based on section 96 and 97, their claims must fail.

The Board therefore rejects their claims.
